name: Eplerenone

lead: Eplerenone is an aldosterone blocker that forum users discuss mainly as a pricier alternative to spironolactone, sometimes with water retention and puffiness in mind.

It blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor so aldosterone cannot drive sodium retention and potassium loss, and it is more receptor-selective than spironolactone. It is approved for hypertension and for heart failure after a heart attack, where the EPHESUS and EMPHASIS-HF trials tested it. Two looksmax.org threads mention it, mostly about cost, and no study has tested it for puffiness.

paras: It is a prescription tablet taken on a schedule set by a doctor for heart failure or blood pressure. In forum discussion it is raised as an option for people who want an aldosterone blocker without spironolactone.
The label's main concern is high potassium and raised creatinine, with higher risk in kidney disease, diabetes and when taken with certain interacting drugs. It is prescription-only in the US.

Help with Oral Compound. What side effects have you gotten?

angle.text: Eplerenone comes up on forums mainly as a costly spironolactone alternative for people who want an aldosterone blocker, sometimes with water retention in mind. By blocking aldosterone it reduces sodium and water retention. It is approved for heart failure and hypertension, with no appearance studies.

lead: Eplerenone (brand name Inspra) is a selective aldosterone receptor antagonist and potassium-sparing diuretic. The US label lists two indications: improving survival in stable adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction after a myocardial infarction, and lowering blood pressure in adults with hypertension.[1][2] Because aldosterone drives sodium and water retention, drugs of this class are discussed in appearance communities as a way to reduce fluid-related facial puffiness (depuffing), and the wiki lists eplerenone as an alternative to spironolactone for that purpose.[3][4]

The reason it is raised as an alternative is its selectivity. Eplerenone was derived from spironolactone and binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with markedly lower affinity than spironolactone, but it has little affinity for androgen, progesterone or glucocorticoid receptors; Wikipedia attributes its lower rate of gynecomastia, impotence and low libido to this selectivity.[3][5] Spironolactone's anti-androgen effects are the reason it is used for acne and hirsutism in women and why men are rarely given it for long periods.[4] People who want an aldosterone blocker without those effects therefore ask about eplerenone.

On looksmax.org the drug turns up in a small number of threads, mostly about what it costs and where to obtain it, and in T Nation threads about managing gynecomastia and blood pressure alongside anabolic regimens.[6][7][8][9] No published study has tested eplerenone for facial puffiness or other appearance outcomes. Its research base is cardiovascular and renal: the EPHESUS and EMPHASIS-HF trials, hypertension studies, and comparisons with the newer non-steroidal agent finerenone.[10][11][12][13] The labelled risk centres on hyperkalemia, and the drug is prescription-only in the United States.[2][3]
infobox: Patented 1983; approved for medical use in the US in 2002[3]
Liver, mainly CYP3A4; no active metabolites identified[2][3]
Community-discussed for depuffing; not studied for it

paras: The US label indicates eplerenone to improve survival in stable adults with symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction after an acute myocardial infarction and to lower blood pressure in adults, alone or with other antihypertensives.[2] Wikipedia also describes its use in heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40 percent or less, where it reduces risk of death and hospitalisation, and in primary hypertension, with spironolactone having more supporting evidence in resistant hypertension.[3] An American Heart Association scientific statement discusses mineralocorticoid antagonists in resistant hypertension, and a European Heart Journal review traces the development of steroidal and non-steroidal antagonists.[14][15]

Eplerenone is also prescribed for central serous chorioretinopathy, an eye condition with subretinal fluid; Wikipedia reports that the largest randomized trial found no significant effect in chronic cases left untreated for four months, while a smaller study in acute cases reported faster fluid resolution than observation.[3]

Within the wiki's depuffing category, eplerenone is listed alongside spironolactone as a diuretic that people discuss for reducing water retention in the face. Spironolactone itself has an established dermatological role: Wikipedia describes it as a first-line anti-androgen for hirsutism in women and as an acne treatment, with improvement taking one to three months for acne and up to six months for hirsutism.[4] Eplerenone is not indicated for those conditions, and the spironolactone article describes eplerenone as lacking spironolactone's anti-androgenic effects.[4]

Spironolactone's anti-androgen action is also the source of its main side effect in men, dose-dependent breast enlargement. In the RALES trial, 9.1 percent of men taking 25 mg a day of spironolactone developed gynecomastia compared with 1.3 percent of controls.[4] This is the context in which eplerenone is raised as a substitute: a T Nation gynecomastia thread notes that eplerenone can be used in place of spironolactone when the latter causes gynecomastia.[8]

Eplerenone binds the mineralocorticoid receptor and blocks aldosterone, which acts in epithelial tissues such as the kidney and in non-epithelial tissues including the heart, blood vessels and brain.[2] In the kidney, blocking aldosterone reduces sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion, lowering blood volume and blood pressure.[3] Wikipedia says its affinity for the receptor is roughly 10 to 20 times lower than spironolactone's, giving an antimineralocorticoid potency of about 50 to 75 percent of spironolactone's; a spironolactone dose of 25 mg per day is described as roughly equivalent to 50 mg per day of eplerenone.[3] A separate overview puts the receptor-affinity difference at 20 to 40 fold, reflecting the 9,11-epoxy group that distinguishes eplerenone's structure.[5]

According to the label, peak plasma levels occur about 1.5 to 2 hours after an oral dose, food does not affect absorption, absolute bioavailability is 69 percent, and the elimination half-life is about 3 to 6 hours with steady state reached within two days.[2] Metabolism is mainly by the liver enzyme CYP3A4 and no active metabolites have been identified.[2] The blood-pressure effect appears within two weeks and is maximal by about four weeks.[2] Wikipedia gives plasma protein binding of about 50 percent and excretion of roughly two thirds in urine and a third in faeces.[3]

The label lists hyperkalemia and raised creatinine as the most common adverse reactions in the post-infarction heart failure population: in EPHESUS, hyperkalemia occurred in 3.4 percent of eplerenone patients versus 2.0 percent on placebo, and increased creatinine in 2.4 versus 1.5 percent.[2] In hypertension trials, overall adverse-event rates were similar to placebo (47 versus 45 percent), while gynecomastia and abnormal vaginal bleeding were reported with eplerenone but not placebo, and became more frequent with longer therapy.[2] Wikipedia states that sexual side effects occur less often than with spironolactone.[3]

The label names hyperkalemia as the main warning. Risk is higher with impaired kidney function, diabetes, proteinuria, and concurrent ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs or moderate CYP3A inhibitors; potassium is measured before starting and checked periodically.[2] Contraindications include serum potassium above 5.5 mEq/L at initiation, creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min or less, and concurrent strong CYP3A inhibitors such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin and ritonavir; additional contraindications apply in hypertension, including potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics.[2]

For pregnancy, human data are insufficient to establish drug-associated risk; animal studies at 31 to 32 times the human exposure from 100 mg per day showed no teratogenic effects, though fetal weights fell and resorptions rose at the highest exposures.[2] Wikipedia's Australian classification is Pregnancy category B3.[3]

The first aldosterone antagonists were identified in the 1950s, and spironolactone was launched in 1959 as a potassium-sparing diuretic after Hans Selye reported that it protected rats from aldosterone-induced cardiac necrosis.[5][4] Further work showed that the receptor also binds cortisol in humans, leading to the name mineralocorticoid receptor, and a second wave of development sought more selective steroidal agents, of which eplerenone was one.[5] Eplerenone was patented in 1983 and approved for medical use in the United States in 2002.[3] In the US, Inspra is sold by Viatris, which took over the Pfizer-linked Upjohn business.[3]

Clinical evidence accumulated through the 2000s and 2010s. EPHESUS (published 2003) tested eplerenone after myocardial infarction with left ventricular dysfunction, and EMPHASIS-HF (2011) enrolled patients with mild systolic heart failure.[10][11] A 2024 individual-patient meta-analysis in The Lancet pooled the RALES and EMPHASIS-HF trials in reduced ejection fraction with trials of spironolactone and finerenone in mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction.[16]

Eplerenone is prescription-only in the United States and Australia (Schedule 4), and is approved in Canada, the European Union, the Netherlands and Japan.[3] Wikipedia estimates its cost at US$2.93 per day for heart failure and US$5.86 per day for hypertension.[3]

In two looksmax.org threads from 2025, users discuss the monthly cost of eplerenone at a 25 mg strength and where it can be sourced. One poster complains that his only source charges about $45 a month, and another says he bought 100 tablets for about $30; neither thread presents studies of eplerenone for appearance.[6][7] The threads are conducted in the site's usual slang and sit alongside discussion of other compounds, so eplerenone is treated as one component of a broader self-directed routine.[7]

On T Nation, a gynecomastia sticky notes eplerenone as the replacement when spironolactone causes gynecomastia, a user in a thread on ageing reports gynecomastia as a side effect that he attributed to eplerenone, and a 2026 thread about the side effects of an oral compound includes a poster suggesting adding nebivolol and eplerenone to a telmisartan regimen to manage rising blood pressure.[8][17][9] These forum comments describe individual experiences and are not clinical guidance; the label lists gynecomastia as an adverse reaction that was reported with eplerenone in hypertension trials.[2]
No studies found on eplerenone for facial puffiness or other cosmetic uses. Related research in other conditions includes the following.

Heart failure: EPHESUS randomised patients with left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction, and EMPHASIS-HF randomised 2,737 patients with NYHA class II systolic heart failure; both are cited as supporting its approved use.[10][11] Wikipedia reports that eplerenone raises left ventricular ejection fraction by an average of 4.95 percentage points and reduces risk of death and hospitalisation.[3] The 2024 Lancet individual-patient meta-analysis examined mineralocorticoid antagonists across the ejection-fraction range.[16]

Hypertension and kidney: The 4E study compared eplerenone, enalapril and their combination in hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy.[12] A randomised study (ARTS-HF) compared finerenone with eplerenone in worsening heart failure with diabetes or chronic kidney disease.[13] A randomised crossover trial in chronic kidney disease compared the albuminuria-lowering effect of dapagliflozin, eplerenone and the two together over 4-week treatment periods.[18]
Eye: A review of pachychoroid diseases, which include central serous chorioretinopathy, describes subretinal fluid as a common feature of these conditions.[19]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, eplerenone appears in a small number of threads about cost and acquisition, and on T Nation it appears in discussions of gynecomastia and blood pressure.[6][7][8][9]

claims.claim: Eplerenone is a gentler alternative to spironolactone for people who want an aldosterone blocker.
Eplerenone is a pricey option; cheaper sources exist.
Eplerenone can reduce water retention in the face.
Eplerenone helps manage blood pressure in androgen-based regimens.

timeline.event: Spironolactone, the first widely used aldosterone antagonist, is discovered; it is introduced in 1959.[4]
The RALES trial of spironolactone reports gynecomastia in 9.1 percent of men versus 1.3 percent of controls.[4]
Eplerenone is approved for medical use in the United States as Inspra.[1][3]
EPHESUS (post-infarction left ventricular dysfunction) and the 4E hypertension study are published.[10][12]
EMPHASIS-HF trial in mild systolic heart failure is published.[11]
Randomised comparison of finerenone with eplerenone in worsening heart failure with diabetes or kidney disease is published.[13]
American Heart Association scientific statement on resistant hypertension discusses mineralocorticoid antagonists.[14]
Lancet individual-patient meta-analysis of mineralocorticoid antagonists across heart-failure ejection fractions.[16]
Two looksmax.org threads discuss eplerenone cost and sourcing.[6][7]
